title: Chapter 62: Sola's Grandchildren, Part 2 of 5: Haverstock
html:
Haverstock stood on a hill.
Lyra saw it from a long way off, from the top of the next rise, as the road came round the shoulder of the hill and the land opened out in front of them. A round green hill, white now with snow on its sides, standing up on its own in the middle of a wide valley, and on the top of it, like a crown on a head, a village. Gray stone houses climbing up the slopes in rings, one row above another, with their turf roofs white and their chimneys smoking. A church tower, square and squat, not much taller than the houses. And on the very top, in the middle, an open space with something standing up in it, too far away to see.
It was a bigger place than Thistle Ford. Three times bigger, perhaps four. There were walls round the fields below it, a patchwork of white squares and gray lines going down every side of the hill to the river at the bottom. There were sheep in some of the fields, gray dots on the white. There was a road going up the hill to the village in long loops, with a cart on it, very small, pulled by something that might have been a pony.
"Haverstock," said Davin. It was the first thing he had said for an hour. He pointed with his stick. "The cross is at the top."
They went down into the valley and across the river, by a stone bridge this time, an old hump-backed bridge with a dip worn in the middle of it by hooves and wheels. Then up the long loops of road toward the village.
The word had come ahead of them. Lyra knew it before they reached the first house.
She did not know how. Perhaps a child had run on ahead over the fields. Perhaps somebody had seen them from a high window, three strangers and Davin and his dog coming over the rise. Perhaps the valley people simply knew things, the way the birds know when a storm is coming. However it had happened, when they came up the last loop of road and in between the first houses of Haverstock, the people were already there.
They were standing in their doorways.
Not in the street. Not crowding. Just standing, quietly, in the doors of their houses, one or two or three in each, with their hands folded or in their pockets or holding a child by the shoulder. Men and women, old and young. They did not say anything. They watched the three strangers come up the street, and when Oren passed their door, they looked at him, and kept looking until he was past.
Lyra felt her back go stiff.
She had walked up a street like this before, with every face turned to watch her. On the Hill. In the autumn, after her father had burned and the house had been sold and the whole of the Crescent knew. She had walked from the Thorne house to the pawnbroker's with a silver candlestick under her coat, and every door had been full of faces, and every face had been looking at her in a particular way. A way she had never forgotten. A sideways, careful, pleased way, as if her falling were a play put on for their amusement.
These faces were not like that.
She looked at them, as she walked, and tried to work out what they were like instead, and could not. They were not pleased. They were not afraid. They were looking at Oren the way people look at a ship coming into harbor after a long time at sea, when they are not yet sure whose ship it is, or who will come down the plank.
She looked at Oren.
He was walking very straight. He had his eyes on the street ahead of him, on Davin's back, and he was not looking at the doorways at all. But the back of his neck, above his collar, had gone dark red, and his good hand was closed tight at his side.
The houses of Haverstock were bigger than the houses of Thistle Ford, and better made. Some of them had two floors. Some of them had glass in their windows, real glass, thick and greenish and full of bubbles, so that the firelight behind it wobbled. The street was cobbled, and the cobbles had been swept, and the snow heaped up against the walls on either side. There was a smell of baking, somewhere. Oat bread. And under it, stronger as they climbed, a sharp hot smell of iron and coal and horse.
"Smithy," said Oren, without turning his head. His voice was not quite steady. "Up there."
They climbed. The street went round the hill in a spiral, the way the road had, and at every turn there were more doors, and more faces in them. A woman with flour on her arms. A very old man in a chair, wrapped in a blanket, put outside his door so that he could see. A young man with a baby on his shoulder. Children everywhere, in bright knitted caps, red and green and yellow and blue, like a box of beads spilled down the street. The children were not quiet like the grown-ups. They were whispering to each other and pointing and running from doorway to doorway to get ahead and look again.
In one doorway, near the top, there was an old man in an army coat.
Lyra saw him first because his coat was not cut down. It was an army coat the way it had been made, long and gray and heavy, with its brass buttons still on it, all of them, polished. The coat was very old. The moths had been at it. There were holes in the skirts and the cuffs were frayed to threads. But the buttons shone. He had shone them that morning. She was sure of it.
He was very old. Older than Granny Abbe, perhaps. He stood very straight in his doorway, with one hand on the door frame to hold himself up, and his face was all bone and white stubble, and his eyes were wet.
As Oren came level with his door, the old man let go of the frame.
He swayed. Then he caught himself, and drew himself up, and lifted his right hand, slowly, shaking, all the way up to the brim of a cap he was not wearing. And he held it there.
A salute.
Oren stopped dead in the street.
The old man was crying. Not making any sound. Just standing there with his hand at his brow and the tears running down into his white stubble, holding the salute, looking at Oren.
Lyra saw Oren's face. She had known him all her life. She had seen him angry and frightened and hurt and drunk, once, at her father's birthday, and singing. She had never seen him look the way he looked now. Like a man who has been handed something precious and does not know what it is, and is terrified of dropping it.
Then Oren's own right hand came up. He did not seem to decide to do it. It came up by itself, the way a soldier's hand does, the way it had done ten thousand times on a parade ground, flat and straight, to his brow.
They stood like that in the swept street, the two of them, the old man in his moth-eaten coat with the polished buttons and the big gray soldier with his arm in a sling. Saluting each other. Neither of them said a word.
Then the old man lowered his hand, and nodded once, and turned, and went back into his house, and shut the door.
Oren stood in the street with his hand still up.
After a while he brought it down. He looked at it, as if it belonged to someone else.
"I don't know him," he said. Very low. To Lyra. "I don't know who he is. I've never seen him."
"I know," said Lyra.
"Then why—"
"I don't know." She took his arm. "Come on. Davin's waiting. The cross is at the top."
Oren let her lead him.
Behind them, Corin had stopped too, in the middle of the street. Lyra looked back and saw him standing very still on his crutch, looking at the shut door of the old man's house. Then he looked up, past the houses, past the top of the hill, at the sky to the north, and his face had the same look on it that it had had at the Two Sisters. Listening. As if somewhere far off, too low to hear, somebody were calling him by name.
The Cross
The top of the hill was flat, and round, and open to the sky.
The houses stopped there. They stood in a ring round the edge of it, facing inward, with their doors toward the middle, like people standing round a fire. The ground inside the ring had been paved, long ago, with big flat stones, and the stones had been swept that morning, so that the snow lay heaped in a low white wall round the edge of the paving and the stones themselves were bare and dark and wet. On one side of the ring stood the squat church. On another, the smithy, with its wide door open and a red glow inside and the ring of a hammer coming out of it, steady and slow. A cold wind blew across the top of the hill from the north. It smelled of iron and coal and snow.
And in the middle of the paving, alone, stood the cross.
It was not what Lyra had expected.
She had seen market crosses before. There was one on the Hill, at the top of the Crescent, a tall slim column of white stone with a little roof on top and a weathervane shaped like a fish. Rich people's children climbed on its steps. This was not like that. This was older, and heavier, and much more plain. It was a thick square pillar of gray stone, as tall as two men, standing on a base of three broad steps. On the top of the pillar there was a cross, a plain one, with short thick arms. In the middle of the cross, where the arms met, a round stone sun had been carved, with rays.
The sun again. The sun from the door of the hall at Thistle Ford. The sun on the banner. The sun Oren had found on the stone in the snow, yesterday, on the left-hand road.
On the steps of the cross there were wreaths. Wreaths of dry heather, brown and purple and gray, tied with strips of cloth. A great many of them. Some were new, still bright. Some were old, so old that they had gone the color of dust and fallen half to pieces, and nobody had taken them away.
And round the base of the pillar, cut into the stone, there were names.
Lyra saw them as she came closer. Rings of them. Four rings, going round all four sides of the square pillar, one above the other, from just above the top step to just below her own shoulder. Small square letters, cut deep, in long lines. The bottom ring was the newest, the sharpest. The top ring was worn so soft by weather and by hands that the letters were hardly more than shadows in the stone.
There must have been hundreds of them. Lyra tried to count the names on one side of one ring and stopped at forty, because there were more than forty, and because she had suddenly understood what they were.
Davin had stopped at the edge of the paving. He would not come any closer. Flint sat down beside him. The boy took his cap off and held it in both hands in front of him.
There was a woman standing on the far side of the cross.
Lyra had not seen her at first. She was dressed all in black, and she was standing so still, close against the stone, that she had looked like part of it. She was tall, and thin, and very upright, as straight as a pike, with a black wool shawl over her head and crossed over her chest and tied behind her. Her face, inside the shawl, was long and lined and very pale. She had a broom in her hand. A small broom, the kind for sweeping a hearth. She had been sweeping the snow off the top step of the cross, Lyra thought, a little at a time, the way someone dusts a room that nobody uses.
She came round the cross toward them.
She did not hurry. She walked the way a person walks in church. When she reached the front of the cross, where they were standing, she stopped on the bottom step, so that she was a little taller than Oren, and she looked at him.
She looked at him for a long time.
She looked at his face, and at his beard, and at the shape of his shoulders, and at the way he stood. She looked at the sling, and the sword. Then she looked at his face again, very closely, the way a woman looks at a piece of cloth in a shop to see if the color is true.
"Aye," she said at last. Quietly. To herself. "Aye. There it is."
Oren did not move.
"I'm Widow Brennock," said the woman. Her voice was low and dry and very clear, with the valley lilt in it, but less than Granny Abbe's, as if she had spent some years somewhere else and brought some of that place's voice home with her. "I keep the cross. My mother kept it before me, and hers before her." She laid the little broom down on the step, carefully, the bristles toward the stone. "Abbe sent word last night. Davin's sister ran it over the top field in the dark." She looked at Oren again. "She said a Vance had come in off the drove road. I said Abbe was getting old. I said there were no Vances left, not in the valleys. I said the last of them went south before the war and never wrote."
"Who did?" said Lyra.
The widow did not look at her.
"Aldric Vance had a son," she said. "He went south to the city as a young man, before the war, to make his fortune, the way young men do. When them in the gray came up the valleys, they wrote to him to come home. He never came. He never wrote back." She was quiet for a moment. "Aldric went into the valley with his sister, the General, and his son was in the city carrying sacks on a dock. That's who."
Oren's good hand had closed.
"My grandfather," he said. His voice was rough. "My father's father. He came from the north. He never said where."
"No," said Widow Brennock. "He wouldn't have." She turned and looked up at the pillar behind her, at the four rings of names going round and round it, worn and sharp, old and new. "These are the ones who went with her. Into the valley. All of them that went from Haverstock, and Thistle Ford, and Coldwell, and Cray, and the farms between. The ones who went and never came back. The ones who went with the General."
She looked back at Oren.
"Your people are on here, Captain," she said. "Find your own."
Marks on a Stone
Oren went up the steps.
He went up slowly, one step and then the next and then the next, the way an old man goes up stairs, though he was not old. At the top he stopped, and stood with the pillar in front of him, so close that his beard almost touched the stone. The four rings of names went round and round in front of his face.
He put out his good hand and laid it flat on the stone.
Lyra saw him do it. She saw his big brown hand, with its broken knuckles and its old white scars, spread out flat on the gray stone among the names, the way her father used to lay his hand flat on a map. She saw the hand move, a little, feeling the letters under the palm. The cuts in the stone. The shapes.
Then she saw him go still.
She knew what it was before she saw his face. She knew because she knew him, and because she had seen it happen once before, not ten days ago, in Madame Hesper's shop, with the shop sign burning backward in the window. He was looking at the names, and they were not names. They were marks. Lines and curves and dots cut in a stone. They meant nothing to him at all.
He had paid his reading away, to hold a door shut against Vivienne's men. He had paid it for her.
His face had gone red. Not pink, the way a face goes pink in the cold. Red, all at once, a dark painful red that started at the collar and went right up into the roots of his gray hair. He did not move his hand. He did not turn round. He stood on the top step with his palm on his own family's names, and stared at them, and could not read one.
The widow was watching him from the bottom step. She did not say anything. She waited.
The square was very quiet. The hammer in the smithy had stopped. Lyra had not noticed it stop. In the doorways round the edge of the square, the people of Haverstock were standing and watching, and nobody spoke. Somewhere a baby began to cry and was hushed.
Oren's shoulders had gone very stiff. Lyra could see the muscles standing out on the back of his neck, above the collar of his coat. He was not going to say it. She knew that. He would stand there until the stone fell down before he would turn round in front of all these people and say, I can't. He would rather be cut. She had seen him cut. He would rather that.
She looked at Corin.
Corin was standing a little way back from the cross, on his crutch. He was not looking at the names. He was looking at Oren, at the back of Oren's red neck, and his face was very still and very sad. He did not move toward the steps. He knew, Lyra thought, that it was not his to do. He did not know her, and he did not know Oren the way she did, and he had read about Oren in a book, but he knew this. That it was not his.
It was hers.
She had promised it. Not to Oren, not out loud. To herself. On Wednesday night, in the crypt, when she had sat on the cold floor and looked at the wandering beetle-track of chalk that was all her hand would make now, and understood. She had thought then: Oren can't read, and I can't write. He's got my hands, and I've got his eyes. She had thought it the way you think a thing you will not say out loud, because it is too sad and too silly both at once.
She went up the steps.
She did not hurry. She did not look at the people in the doorways. She went up the three broad steps of the cross the way the widow had walked across the square, as if she were in church, and she came and stood beside Oren on the top step, close, with her shoulder against his arm.
He did not look at her.
"Which side?" she said. Quietly. Just to him.
For a moment he did not answer. Then he said, very low, without moving his hand, "I don't know."
"All right." She looked at the stone. At the rings of letters, small and square and deep, going round. She had always been a good reader. Her mother had taught her, before she went away. Her mother had sat with her by the nursery fire every evening, with a book on her knee, and pointed to the letters one by one with a long finger in a gray kid glove. Lyra did not remember that anymore. She had given that memory away too, she thought, or else it had simply gone, the way things go. But the reading had stayed. The reading was in her eyes and not in her hands, and she had not paid with her eyes.
She looked at the names.
They were all sorts of names. Farm names and family names and plain first names on their own. Tam Coldwell. Margery of the Cray Farm. Old Huw. Jenet Ash. She went along the bottom ring, quickly, looking, on the side that faced the church. Then round the corner, onto the side that faced north.
And there, halfway along the second ring, she found them.
They were all together. That was the first thing she saw. Whoever had cut the names had put the families together, the way you put your own people together at a table, and on the north side of the cross, in the second ring, there was a long line of names that all ended the same way.
Vance. Vance. Vance.
She drew in her breath.
Oren heard it. He turned his head, at last, and looked at her, and his face was still red, but there was something else in it now. Something like a man waking up.
"Here," said Lyra. She took his good hand off the stone, gently, by the wrist, the way you lift a child's hand off a hot stove. She moved it round the corner of the pillar, to the north side, to the second ring, and laid it flat again on the stone. Under his palm, the first of the long line of names that all ended the same way.
"Here," she said again. "They're all here, Oren. Together."
He looked at his hand on the stone. He looked at the marks under it.
"Read them to me," he said.
